He'd tell you to raise your prices first, and only then go after more clients. At $35k a month with four people, the quickest way to grow is to make each client worth more. More clients at today's prices would mostly mean more work for the same small team.

He splits "grow" into two levers: get more customers, or make each one worth more [1]. In every consult his first question is whether the business is limited by supply or by demand [2]. A four-person agency bringing in about $8,750 per person per month usually runs out of delivery capacity before it runs out of leads. His rule for that case is "when you have demand, cut supply," so you raise the price rather than add volume [3]. He calls charging more one of the biggest levers a small business has. That's because a higher price raises clients' belief that you can actually deliver, so it can lift your close rate instead of lowering it [4][5]. He also says higher prices bring more committed clients, better results and less demanding customers [5].

Use his test before you set the number. If you close 80% or more of the prospects you pitch, you're underpriced. In the case he worked through, he raised the price about 10% and noted that as long as more than 65% still closed, the business made more money [6]. Work out your own break-even close rate the same way, then raise prices on new clients first. Two more of his moves fit an agency well:
- **Charge more by targeting better clients.** At a PR company he invested in, he found that the 15% of clients who bought the top package also stayed. He rebuilt the business around just that group and raised prices 10x [7]. Look for your best-fit 15%.
- **Add a premium tier at roughly 10x your normal retainer**, even if hardly anyone buys it. It makes the standard package look cheaper by comparison, and the few who do buy it add a lot of profit [8].

He never talked about agencies specifically, so this applies his general pricing and "find the constraint" rules to your situation. Here's what would change his answer. If your team has spare capacity and your close rate is already low, you're limited by demand, not supply. Then he'd say fix the offer and get more out of the lead sources you already have before you add new ones [9]. And once higher prices have filled your team, he'd call running out of capacity "a problem I'd love to create" [10]. At that point the extra margin pays for hiring and for winning more clients.

**Spend it on ads, but don't hire the salesperson yet.** Hormozi would first ask whether you're short on customers or short on capacity. For most small cleaning businesses the answer is customers. He would also want the cheap fixes made before you spend real money on ads. In his view a salesperson is the answer to a different problem: having more leads than you can handle.

He opens every consult with one question: is this business limited by supply or by demand? He warns that owners often "fix" a problem in a way that makes their real constraint worse [1][2]. A salesperson with no extra leads to work just splits the calls you already get. His closest case is a duct-cleaning company doing about $1.25M a year. He ranked its moves in this order: raise prices 10%, keep paying down debt, build a dedicated ad landing page, fix the ad creative, then raise ad spend. He put that order first because better ads and a better page alone "might already double or triple your lead flow." Then the owner might not need to spend more at all, and would instead find he doesn't "have enough guys," which Hormozi calls a problem he'd "love to create" [3]. Hiring comes after the leads, not before.

Here's how that applies to your $10k. First check your price: if you close 80% or more of quotes, you're probably underpriced, and a raise pays off as long as you still close above 65% [4]. Next, put up a simple landing page that leads with your offer. Test ad ideas as free organic posts first and turn the winners into paid ads [5]. Then spend in steps rather than all at once. Keep raising the budget month over month as long as your cost per customer and return on ad spend hold [6]. If you can't tell which customers came from the ads, that's "a data problem," so fix your tracking before you spend more [7]. Cleaning works well for this because it's recurring. Each new customer is worth many visits, so you can afford to pay more to win one.

A few things would change his answer. If you already have more leads than you can call back or quote, you're limited by sales capacity. Then he'd tell you to add salespeople, as he told a business drowning in about 300 leads a day [8]. And if you or someone on your team can reliably close by knocking doors, he'd go "all in door to door." That means building a commission-paid canvassing team on top of what already works, rather than learning ads from scratch [9].

He'd tell you to cut it down. Adding more workouts and content is the opposite of what he'd do. He says the top reason people cancel, after price, is overwhelm, "and this is why doing less can often retain more" [1]. When a member pays for five things and uses one, they feel they're getting 20% of the value. Offer just that one thing at the same price and they feel they're getting 100% [2]. Every workout or video they skip makes them feel they're wasting money, so each new one is another reason to cancel [3].

His main example is from fitness. Planet Fitness surveyed gym members and found that most of them "just used the cardio equipment and a little bit of weights" [4]. So it dropped everything else and charged $10 a month. He also mentions an online community that deleted content and cut monthly churn from 30% to 5%. That's about six times the customer lifetime value, just from offering less [5]. In 2025 he made the same cut in his own paid community, where overwhelm was the top reason people cancelled. He went from three calls a week to one and moved the big monthly download to quarterly [6].

What he'd have you do:
- **Find out what people really use.** Ask members which one thing they'd fight to keep if you deleted everything else, and which one thing they wouldn't miss. Focus on the top one or two [7].
- **Give busy members one clear path.** Build a "start here" page and a weekly routine, and keep the extra content optional as "side quests" [8]. Most of your members aren't working out with you full-time. They need value fast.
- **Get new members a quick win.** Ideally they get one within 24 hours [9]. Your first three months are where most people leave, so make sure that by day 90 they can see a real change in their fitness [10].
- **Check why people leave.** Message everyone who cancels, record the reason, and every 20 or so cancellations fix the top one or two reasons [11].

This is close to a direct answer from him (he talked about a gym, and about online programs that deleted content). What would change it: if your cancellation reasons turn out to be mostly price, or "I didn't get results," the fix is your price or your program's core promise, not how much is in it. Even then, he'd fix the one thing that delivers the result before adding anything new.

**Keep the job for now.** Hormozi would tell you to build the business in the hours around your 9-to-5, cut your spending hard, and bank cash. You quit once the business and your savings can carry the risk. Quitting just to prove you're committed isn't how he thinks about it.

He says your nine-to-five "is not killing your dreams" [1]. What's wasted is the two four-hour blocks around it: 5 to 9 in the morning and 5 to 9 at night [2]. Use those blocks for selling and delivering, not for watching more content. He also argues that a job is not riskier than owning a business. He calls that idea a myth spread by "entrepreneur talking heads", and says employment is the lowest-risk way to make money [3]. So the salary isn't something to escape. It's what pays for your early attempts.

Money is the second reason. His first step for anyone starting out is to cut every cost "so that we can take more risk" [4]. That means roommates or living with family, a paid-off car, and no lifestyle upgrades. He's blunt that "you cannot take any risk on if you have no time and no money" [5]. His checkpoint is $100K in the bank, not $100K in revenue [6]. He says he felt richest when he first had that much, because he stopped worrying about rent and could think long-term. He never named an exact point at which to quit. By his rules, though, you'd go all in once the side business shows real paying demand and you have a year or more of savings. Then the downside is capped and the upside isn't, which he calls "the recipe for opportunity" [7].

Here's what would change his answer. He did quit outright himself, at 22, and calls it the hardest decision of his life. He did it because he hated the job, and he says that if he'd liked it he'd never have left [8]. If what's really keeping you there is other people's expectations, his line is that sometimes you have to let their dreams for your life die so yours can live [9]. If you're under 30 with no dependents, he'd also push you to work as many hours as you can, because you'll never have fewer responsibilities than you do now [10]. And if your current life doesn't feel like a cage, he'd say maybe it isn't one, and you could just enjoy it [11].

**Offer a guarantee, but make it conditional on the client doing the work, and use it to justify a higher price than $2,000.** He wouldn't tell you to go no-refunds just to protect cash. To him, how sure the buyer is that they'll get the result is part of what they're paying for, and a guarantee is one of the most direct ways to raise that.

Perceived likelihood of achievement is one of the four parts of his value equation. In his ideal offer, the buyer is "virtually guaranteed" to get the outcome [1]. On deal structure he says plainly that "you can absolutely sell a guarantee" [2]. Taking on the risk that "something goes wrong" is something you can choose to do "for a premium" [3]. He uses this himself: his service-business example is a priority fee that is refunded in full if the deadline is missed [4]. So a guarantee isn't a giveaway. You carry the risk the buyer is worried about, and you charge for carrying it. He adds a limit: you can only take on that risk "when you're good" [5]. If your program doesn't reliably get results, the guarantee will lose you money, and that tells you to fix the delivery, not to hide behind a no-refunds policy.

For a $2,000 coaching program, write the conditions so they also push commitment. For example: attend every call, do the assignments, and if you haven't hit the agreed result by day 90, you get your money back. Or offer to keep coaching them free until they hit it. He makes the same point about price: higher prices "increase the emotional investment" and lower how demanding clients are [6]. Conditions do that too. The clients who meet them are the ones who get results, so very few of them claim the refund.

**What would change his answer**
- **Your reputation already does the job.** He calls reputation "almost an implied guarantee" [7]. If you have strong proof and referrals, an explicit guarantee adds less.
- **You're already closing most of your calls.** His rule is to fix the offer only when too few people say yes [8]. If you're closing 80%+ of calls, he'd raise the price before adding a guarantee.
- **Strict no-refunds can work, but only as a deliberate stance.** In *$100M Offers* (outside the vault) he presents "no refunds" as a legitimate guarantee type when it's framed as a reason, such as "we only take committed people." He doesn't present it as a default way to avoid risk.

**He'd tell you to pay off the credit cards first and the car loan next. Then put what's left into the business, but only into spending that has already shown it pays back. Don't put all of it in.**

Hormozi never talked about this exact choice, but his rules on it are clear. He says he leans "very close to the Ramsey side" on debt. His reason is that debt adds risk, and risk held for a long time tends to come due, because businesses have seasons and swings [1][2]. When a business owner he was advising said they'd pay off $60k of debt in four to five months, he approved and made it the second item on their priority list. He even admitted the payoff is partly emotional, to get it out of the back of your mind [1]. His wider rule is to get yourself "out of the hole as fast as humanly possible" so you can think long-term, because you can't hold a vision while bills are due [3]. Credit card debt is that hole. His ideal car is "a paid-off clunker" [4]. So pay the car off, or if the payment is large, sell the car and buy something cheap with cash.

This isn't him being against risk. He thinks most people take too little. But he says the first step is to cut costs "so that we can take more risk", and that you can't take risk if you have no time and no money [5][6]. Once the monthly card and car payments are gone, you keep more cash every month, and that cash becomes your fuel for risk. The money that goes into the business should go to his three categories: tools, help with implementation (ideally one-on-one), and trial attempts such as ad tests [7]. Only scale spending where returns are proven. His rule for ads is to keep spending as long as cost per customer and return on ad spend hold at break-even or better [8]. Putting everything into a business that hasn't proven its numbers is the kind of Hail Mary he warns against.

**What would change his answer:** if the business already has a channel that reliably makes back more than it costs, he'd fund that hard, though probably still after clearing the high-interest cards. His own history is also less tidy than his advice. When he had lost almost everything, he ran his comeback on a credit card with a $100k limit [9]. He calls that move his "one hail Mary play", not a recommendation.

He never talks about Black Friday or holiday sales directly, so this comes from his pricing rules. They all point the same way. His view is that price tells the buyer how likely the thing is to work. When he raises prices, customers become more confident he can deliver, more emotionally invested, and less demanding [1]. For owners under about $3–5M in revenue, he calls charging more one of the biggest levers they have. A 30% cut sends that signal in reverse. It also brings in the buyers who care most about price, when he wants the ones who value the result most. He says that when people who aren't your ideal customer call you too expensive, you ignore them, because "the price is actually acting as a good filter" [2].

Urgency is where your Black Friday instinct is right, but he would only use it if it's real. A reason to act now works even when the reason is thin, and it works better when it's tied to a deadline [3]. But the deadline has to hold: when it passes, you say no. If buyers learn that a 30% sale comes around every November, they stop buying at full price and wait, and your deadlines lose "power" [4]. So keep the price and use the date to make the offer better. Add something that only buyers this week get, close it at a deadline that actually holds, and stick to it. (He's also known for saying "add bonuses, don't discount" in his book *$100M Offers*. That's from outside his talks here, but it fits this advice.)

Before you change price in either direction, he'd want you to check the break-even point. That's how he decided on a 10% price rise for a client: he worked out that they made more money as long as more than 65% of prospects still closed [1]. Here's the same check run on your discount. A course costs almost nothing per extra copy, so at 30% off you'd need about 43% more buyers just to bring in the same revenue (1 ÷ 0.7 ≈ 1.43). You'd also carry the long-term cost of teaching your audience to wait for sales.

Two things would change his answer:

- **The course is sold as a subscription.** The one discount he recommends is a discounted annual plan, around 16–17% ("buy 10 get two"), because yearly buyers decide once instead of twelve times and cancel less [5].

**He'd tell you not to sell at 3x profit, at least not the whole thing and not yet.** Three times profit means the buyer gets their money back in three years and keeps every dollar after that. If you hold on, you collect the same money over those three years and you still own the business. He'd call taking the cheque now a shortcut, and he has said that "poor people stay poor because they want a fast way to get rich." His rule is to pick one path and stay on it for about a decade [1]. If you built this business yourself, one of its main advantages, in his words, is that you can exit "on your own time horizon or never exit at all." The point is to build something that compounds and let time do the work [2].

Before you think about selling, he'd have you raise what the business is worth. A business is worth more when it has more customers or each customer is worth more. Recurring revenue is "significantly more valuable" than one-off sales [3], and he gets there with steady small improvements, not big gambles. His own sale shows how he'd do it. He and Leila took $42M out of the companies as profit along the way, and then sold only two-thirds of them for $46.2M [4][5]. They kept a third and got paid twice. Also think about what you'd do with the cash. He called the family-office years after the sale the "most chill" period of his life, then went back to running companies anyway [6]. He also says that living off investments is the slowest path and that almost nobody gets rich that way unless they already have a high income [6]. If you have no next project and wouldn't be happy retired, the money will just sit there and earn less than the business does.

He'd change his answer in three cases:
- **You're in financial trouble.** If you're deep in debt or have no cash cushion, take the money and "get yourself out of the hole" [7]. Safety comes first for him.
- **The business carries risk that will catch up with you.** That could be heavy debt, a market that's shrinking, or a business that only works because you're there every day. For him, risk "tends to come due" over time [8].
- **You have a much bigger idea that needs the cash.** If that's true, focus on the bigger bet, because compounding only works if you say no to everything else [9]. Even then, he'd look at selling a majority stake while keeping some equity before selling all of it.

He never talked about a specific 3x offer, so this is applied from his rules about compounding, safety and focus, plus how he handled his own sale.

Hormozi would tell you not to learn to code. First check whether you need a custom app at all. If you do, pay someone good to build it and spend your own hours selling and delivering.

**Start by asking whether the app is your bottleneck.** In every consult he first asks whether the business is short of customers or short of capacity to serve them, and then he works only on that [1]. Most small businesses are short of customers, and an app rarely fixes that. His daily split is promote, deliver, build, with promotion first, because "if nobody knows about your stuff, they can't give you money" [2].

**Then look for a tool that already exists.** When he lists where early money should go, the first bucket is tools like a CRM or a landing-page builder. The alternative, in his words, is to "rebuild the entire thing" when you could "grab a tool that's already there. Save yourself some time" [3]. An off-the-shelf subscription with a few workarounds beats any custom build, whether you write it or hire it out.

**If it really has to be custom, hire.** He never talked about AI coding tools specifically, but his rules settle this. Learning to build software is a second big project that competes with the business that pays you. He says "the price of wanting to be good at everything is being good at nothing" [4]. He admits that starting a second approach before the first has paid off is his own worst habit, because it "ends up just pulling resources from the one way that I know will work" [5]. He also calls switching between tasks "the biggest killer of productivity" [6], and you'd be switching between running the business and debugging code. He describes his own goal as being "decent enough" at each business function that none of them holds the business back, not being great at all of them [7]. So know enough about the app to judge whoever builds it, and leave the building to them. When he does want a skill himself, his shortcut is still to "hire them one-on-one" [8].

**What would change his answer:** If the app is the product you sell, and not a tool your business uses, then building it is your one big bet. He grants that software businesses can now be started cheaply on your own money ("now it kind of is") [9], and he values stacking skills [10]. In that case he'd have you learn it through sheer volume of attempts, with an expert coaching you. Even then, he'd want proof that people will pay before you build much.
